options: AWS's managed service for running Apache Kafka
A rebranded version of Kinesis Data Streams
Microsoft's streaming service inside Fabric
A SQL query engine for Kafka topics
questions.explain: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Kafka) handles broker provisioning and patching for Apache Kafka while leaving you the standard Kafka topic/partition model.

questions.q: What is Kafka's equivalent of a Kinesis shard?
options: A partition (inside a topic)
A bucket
A Lambda function
A delivery stream
questions.explain: Kafka organizes data into topics divided into partitions — conceptually the same role a shard plays inside a Kinesis stream.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of choosing Kinesis over Kafka/MSK?
options: Kinesis has less operational overhead but is AWS-only, while Kafka is portable across clouds with a larger ecosystem
Kinesis is open-source, while Kafka is proprietary to AWS
Kinesis cannot integrate with Lambda or S3
Kafka cannot be run on AWS in any form
questions.explain: Kinesis trades portability for a fully managed, low-friction AWS-native experience; Kafka trades some operational simplicity for portability and a bigger connector ecosystem.

options: Microsoft Fabric's managed real-time ingestion service, integrated with OneLake and Power BI
An AWS service for streaming data into Redshift
A Kafka distribution maintained by Microsoft
A feature of Kinesis Data Analytics
questions.explain: Fabric Eventstreams is Microsoft's equivalent to Kinesis — a managed streaming ingestion service that routes data natively into Fabric's OneLake, KQL databases, and Power BI.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should mainly drive the choice between Kinesis, Kafka/MSK, and Fabric Eventstreams?
options: What the rest of the data platform already looks like, not which service is abstractly 'best'
Whichever service is cheapest per gigabyte in every scenario
Always choosing Kafka, since it's open-source
Always choosing the newest service released by any vendor
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that the right streaming service usually follows the platform decision already made — AWS-native, Kafka-committed, or Fabric-standardized — rather than a context-free 'best' pick.
